Spinal nerve ROOTS vs BRANCHES (rami): DORSAL ROOT = sensory only (cell bodies in the dorsal root ganglion) · VENTRAL ROOT = motor only (cell bodies in the spinal cord). After the roots join, the DORSAL BRANCH and VENTRAL BRANCH are both MIXED (slides 8, 10). Dorsal root ≠ dorsal ramus.

Gray matter map (slide 9): SOMATIC afferent = MEDIAL dorsal horn · VISCERAL afferent = LATERAL dorsal horn · VISCERAL efferent = LATERAL horn (specific regions only) · SOMATIC efferent = VENTRAL horn.

Cord SEGMENT ≠ VERTEBRA: segments are shorter than their vertebrae, so the cord ends before the vertebral canal does and the caudal roots run caudally to reach their foramen (cauda equina) (slides 15–16). Dog cord ends far more caudally than the human cord (L1/L2, slide 18).

Caudal cord, cranial → caudal: CONUS MEDULLARIS (tapering cord) → FILUM TERMINALE (fibrous band to periosteum of the caudal vertebrae). CAUDA EQUINA = the NERVES (last lumbar, sacral, caudal), not part of the cord itself (slide 16).
Spaces, outside → in: EPIDURAL (outside dura) → SUBDURAL → SUBARACHNOID (CSF; where myelogram contrast goes) (slides 16, 26, 42). Epidural = anesthesia space; subarachnoid = CSF tap / contrast space.

CSF tap sites: CEREBELLOMEDULLARY cistern = needle through the ATLANTO-OCCIPITAL membrane (slide 29) vs LUMBOSACRAL interarcuate space (slides 16–17). Don't mix the membrane (atlanto-occipital, skull–atlas) with the dorsal ATLANTOAXIAL ligament (atlas–axis).

Long ligaments: SUPRASPINOUS (tips of spinous processes, thoracic + lumbar) · DORSAL LONGITUDINAL (floor of the vertebral canal, AXIS → SACRUM) · VENTRAL LONGITUDINAL (ventral surface of bodies, MID-THORAX → SACRUM) (slide 34). Dorsal longitudinal is INSIDE the canal — directly between disk and cord.

Short ligaments: INTERSPINOUS = between spinous processes · INTERARCUATE = between vertebral arches (= ligamentum flavum on the human figure, slide 18 — outside knowledge, confirm) · INTERTRANSVERSE = between transverse processes (slides 35–36). Supraspinous (long, along the tips) ≠ interspinous (short, between processes).
NUCHAL ligament (axis spine → T1 spine in the dog figure, slide 33) is NOT the ligamentum flavum/interarcuate ligament (between arches, roof of the canal).
Disk: ANNULUS FIBROSUS = OUTER fibrocartilage · NUCLEUS PULPOSUS = INNER soft part that HERNIATES when the annulus ruptures (slide 39).

Thoracic disks herniate dorsally less often → the INTERCAPITAL ligament (rib head to rib head, dorsal to the disk, ventral to the dorsal longitudinal ligament) (slides 37, 39C, 44 — answer not printed on slide; confirm).

Horner's: preganglionic sympathetics for the eye leave at T1 and pass THROUGH the cervicothoracic and middle cervical ganglia WITHOUT synapsing; synapse = CRANIAL CERVICAL ganglion. T1 avulsion (proximal to the communicating branch) = Horner's; lesion of the ventral branch DISTAL to the communicating branch = NO Horner's (slide 57).

⚠️ FLAG (slide 6 clicker, no answer key on slide): 'Which region has a different number of segments than vertebrae?' Outside knowledge (confirm): dog has 8 cervical segments vs 7 cervical vertebrae, and ~5 caudal segments vs ~20 caudal vertebrae — so both A (cervical) and E (caudal) differ; cervical is the classic answer. Confirm with transcript.

⚠️ FLAG (segments for eye sympathetics): slide 57 says T1 '(maybe T2 as well)'; the figure caption on slide 54 says the first 3 thoracic segments (T1, T2, T3); slide 8 marks preganglionic sympathetic cell bodies as T1–L4(5). Use T1 (± T2) per the professor's bullet until the transcript confirms.

⚠️ FLAG (spelling for Canvas): slide 15 bullet writes 'intumescense' (singular) and the figure writes 'intumescence'; slide 17 title says 'Cauda equine'; slide 58 says 'nasocilliary'. Standard spellings (outside knowledge): intumescentia / intumescence, cauda equina, nasociliary nerve.

⚠️ FLAG (ptosis mechanism, slide 60): slide says ptosis comes from loss of sympathetic tone in eyelid smooth muscle, but also notes some argue that muscle is minor in veterinary species and ptosis is secondary to enophthalmos. Both versions on the slide — confirm which the professor wants.
